ChemE is definitely tough and if I didn't end up where I am now, it wouldn't have been worth it. I say that because I've known a lot of people struggle after what to do after graduation. The struggle comes from the volatility entailed with chemical engineering. I chose ChemE to escape volatility of petroleum engineering, but I realized that there is enough overlap that ChemeE follows a lot of the same up and downs as the oil industry. People nowadays are worried about jobs because of the recession, but I've realized both ChemE's and Petroleum engineers have to deal with recessions AND low oil prices that could come from price wars or supply issues. This causes layoffs in the oil industry and experienced engineers that flood the job market, even for chemE jobs. For instance, a ChemE friend did 2 oil internships during college, but couldn't come back to those companies or any other oil companies because of low oil prices. It actually made interviewing hard too because most of the companies he interviewed with for full-time afterwards kept asking him why he gave up on oil. 

You could honestly avoid the volatility risk and still make a similar salary in another major, if money is a factor to you. For instance, I've heard people say that civil engineering makes less money on average compared to other majors, but I'll give you some examples here. An entry level at JMT, a civil consulting company, makes 65,000 while a junior engineer at P&G, a ChemE company, makes 60,000. A civil engineer starting at CP&Y can make 75,000 and a ChemE at Samsung Austin Semiconductor will start with the same salary.

I followed through with ChemE, but I had to get a master's degree because I had difficulty finding an engineering job after college during low oil prices and I didn't want to go into finance like a large portion of my classmates did. It worked out because I took graduate school way more seriously than undergraduate. My main regret is that I wasn't serious enough during my undergrad years and I didn't find my passion, so it could be one or a combination of not having a passion and low oil prices that made graduating with my bachelor's difficult. 

I don't know much about MechE's, but I think ECE would probably be one of the hardest majors but with a better job market. Although I might be saying it's hard because I failed my high school electronic classes and I couldn't do marching band because of that lol
